summary: Describes how several Source Address Validation Improvement methods can coexist on one device when a network uses different address assignment techniques, and how conflicts are resolved when two methods find the same binding.

plainLanguage.summary: Different guards check ID in different ways. This explains how they work together and settle disagreements.

questions: how do savi methods work together
subtitle: How several source address validation methods share one binding table and settle conflicts.

tldr.problem: A network switch may need several Source Address Validation Improvement (SAVI) methods at once, one per address assignment technique, and each would otherwise reject addresses the others learned or collide over the same address.
tldr.mechanism: A mechanism called SAVI-MIX arbitrates between the methods: they share one binding table, and SAVI-MIX resolves conflicts using first-come first-served with a few exceptions.
tldr.outcome: The RFC recommends keeping address spaces separate so collisions do not happen, and gives preference rules for when they do. Combining methods does not improve each method's security.

facts.label: Lifetime priority
facts.value: Manual, then SAVI-DHCP, then FCFS SAVI

today: RFC 8074 is a Standards Track document, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction and Problem Scope
sections.content:
Several SAVI documents describe how a switch learns and records bindings between a node's IP address and a binding anchor, then uses them to validate source addresses. RFC 6620 covers StateLess Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC, FCFS SAVI), RFC 7513 covers DHCP, and RFC 7219 covers Secure Neighbor Discovery (SEND). Each deals with collisions on its own.

All assignment techniques can coexist within a layer 2 domain, and a SAVI device MUST implement the SAVI method for each technique in use. A fourth technique, manual binding configuration, needs no new method because operators decide how to manage it. Without coordination each method would reject addresses it did not discover, so the binding table SHOULD be shared by all methods in use. Collisions inside one method are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: A school has several guards, each knowing kids from a different list. If each only trusts their own list, they turn away kids the other guards let in. So they should share one list.

sections.title: SAVI-MIX Architecture
sections.content:
SAVI-MIX acts as an arbiter of the binding generation algorithms of the methods. When a method produces a candidate binding, it asks SAVI-MIX to set up the entry. SAVI-MIX checks the binding table for a conflict: with none, the binding is created; with one, it decides to replace the existing binding or reject the candidate, following the policies in Section 6.

Packet filtering is then based on the combined table rather than on each method separately. Each entry holds the IP source address, the binding anchor (RFC 7039), the lifetime, the creation time and the binding method that created it. The filtering details are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: A head guard collects suggestions from each guard, checks for clashes, and writes the final list everyone uses.

sections.title: Avoiding Collisions by Separating Assignment
sections.content:
If each assignment technique uses its own part of the address space, collisions will not happen, so non-overlapping address space is recommended.

  • DHCP and SLAAC: use non-overlapping prefixes. Set the A bit in the Prefix Information option of the Router Advertisement for the SLAAC prefix, and set the M bit in the Router Advertisement for the DHCP prefix.
  • SEND and non-SEND: avoid mixed environments, or separate the prefixes announced to SEND and non-SEND nodes, for example with unicast Router Advertisements (RFC 6085) answering SEND and non-SEND Router Solicitations.
sections.plainLanguage: Give each guard their own set of classrooms, and no two guards ever argue about the same kid.

sections.title: Resolving Collisions on Different Anchors
sections.content:
When one address is bound to two different anchors by different methods, for example SLAAC on node X (anchor-X) and later DHCP on node Y (anchor-Y), the device must choose. A manually configured binding is preferred (SHOULD). Otherwise the device SHOULD choose the first-come anchor, whatever method learned it, because the SLAAC, DHCP and SEND specifications already imply first-come, first-served.

There are two exceptions. With Cryptographically Generated Addresses (CGA), preference goes to the anchor carrying verified CGA credentials; an attacker replaying them competes on a first-come basis. The second is configuration: an operator may configure a triplet of prefix or address, anchor and method (at least one of anchor and method MUST be given). If a Duplicate Address Detection message arrives for a target not in the binding table, inside the configured prefix, with a different anchor than configured, and the configured method is not FCFS SAVI, the switch SHOULD defend the address with a Neighbor Advertisement, SHOULD NOT install the entry, and SHOULD discard the DAD message rather than forward it. Rate-limiting the defense advertisements is suggested.

With several SAVI devices, DAD across the perimeter informs all of them, so first-come, first-served works as with one switch. Preferences on all devices in the layer 2 domain should be consistent, since inconsistent settings may cause network breaks.
sections.plainLanguage: If two kids claim the same locker, the first one who got it keeps it. Teachers can write down special cases, such as a locker always reserved for the principal.

sections.title: Same Address on the Same Anchor
sections.content: A binding can also be set up on the same anchor by multiple methods, typically FCFS SAVI and SAVI-DHCP. If their lifetimes differ, priority goes to 1) manual configuration, 2) SAVI-DHCP, and 3) FCFS SAVI as the least authoritative. The binding is removed when the prioritized lifetime expires, even if a less authoritative method had a longer lifetime.
sections.plainLanguage: If two lists say the same kid is allowed in until different times, trust the more official list.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
Combining SAVI methods does not improve or remove the security considerations of each method, which still apply as described in each method's RFC. Two additional effects exist. The binding setup rate is the sum of the rates of all enabled methods, so susceptibility to DoS attacks may increase and implementers must account for the resources. And because several mechanisms are supported, the security level may drop to that of the weakest method unless extra steps such as non-overlapping address spaces are taken.

Privacy considerations of all methods apply cumulatively. The document requires no IANA registrations.
sections.plainLanguage: A fence is only as strong as its weakest board, and more guards means more paperwork to handle.
